newsitem.title: FRANCE: Union battles loom over French railways, power.
newsitem.headline: Union battles loom over French railways, power.

text.p: Labour battles loomed on Monday at two of France's biggest state companies, with unions unhappy over government reform plans for the SNCF railways and at odds over proposals to cut working hours at EDF-GDF power utility.

The Communist-led General Labour Confederation (CGT), the biggest union at state utility Electricite de France and Gaz de France, called a 24-hour strike on Wednesday over plans to cut the working week to between 32 and 35 hours from 38 in order to prevent job cuts.
Three other unions endorsed the plan while a fourth, Workers Force (FO), agreed to discuss it further on a regional basis.

The strike threat at EDF-GDF was made on the eve of a Senate debate on a controversial government rescue plan for the state railways which is opposed by two key unions, and as unrest loomed in a host of other sectors.

Train drivers in the CFDT union, France's biggest, have appealed for a nationwide rail strike on January 31 in protest at the overhaul which is part of Prime Minister Alain Juppe's reform drive. Unions say it could lead to job losses.

Unions in other sectors, encouraged by truckers winning the right to retire at 55 after a crippling 12-day strike in November, have been scrambling to jump on the bandwagon and win similar government concessions.

In Paris, Credit Foncier bank officials were held hostage by employees for a fourth day on Monday in a standoff with the government over job security and the bank's fate. Urban transport workers outside Paris plan a stoppage on Friday.
Plans at EDF-GDF are to allow workers to work 32 hours a week for three years and be paid for 35 hours, or work 35 hours and be paid for 36.5 hours.

The management says the plan will allow to maintain staffing levels over the next three years. It says that, otherwise, the utility would lose up to 6,000 jobs, hiring 5,000 to 7,000 new staff while 11,000 staff retire.
CGT said the plan was disastrous for employment and wages and called a strike to force the government to accept to cut working hours without cutting salaries.
At SNCF, the head of CGT's rail branch, Bernard Thibault, accused the government of planning to shed thousands of jobs.
He said the CGT would decide in the next few days whether to call a strike.
Memories are still vivid of a 1995 strike by railway and other public transport workers which paralysed the country for more than three weeks just ahead of the Christmas holiday.

"Things are going to be a bit bumpy," said one Juppe aide of the labour turbulence partly prompted by the premier yielding to truckers' demands for early retirement, shorter working hours and higher pay.
Six of eight trade unions are ready to back the SNCF reform which would create a state company to take over 134.2 billion francs ($24.87 billion) of SNCF debts totalling 208 billion.

SNCF chairman Louis Gallois, in an interview with the daily Le Parisien, said the overhaul would benefit travellers who in some cases would see cheaper fares, and pledged that rail staff would not lose their benefits.
"Without the reform, the SNCF would be asphyxiated...We'll try to provide a better service at a lower cost," he said.
Transport Minister Bernard Pons ruled out last week delaying the SNCF reform because of a strike threat. The plan has already been put on hold last November in a bid to appease unions.

The new state company, likely to be called France Rail, would become owner of the infrastructure and charge the SNCF, which would continue as railways operator and maintain the infrastructure, fees for use of Europe's biggest rail network.

The Socialist CFDT and Communist-led CGT unions argue that the split amounts to a break-up and a precursor to opening France's railways to competition. But they have not yet hit on a common strategy to combat it.
